transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Yeah, um… I came in because I just feel like I can’t shut off. Like I’m constantly running on a motor lately. I’ll finish something at school, or at home, and before I even take a breath I’m onto the next thing.

I’m a special education teacher, so there’s always something to do anyway, you know—papers, kids needing help, emails, and then I get home and it’s the same kind of thing, just different tasks. But it feels like it’s more than just being busy. It’s like my body and brain won’t let me stop moving from one thing to the next.
Do you often find yourself talking more than others in social situations?

Yeah… yeah, I do. I don’t always realize it in the moment, but I’ll go into, say, a parent conference or a staff meeting thinking, “Okay, just keep it short,” and then suddenly I’m giving three examples, then I’m telling some story from my classroom, then I’m offering ideas nobody even asked for.

And I can kind of see the other person doing that thing where they’re ready to wrap up—looking at the clock or shifting papers—but I’m still talking. It’s embarrassing afterward, because I really didn’t mean to take over the conversation.
Do you often interrupt others when they're speaking?

Yeah, I do… more than I’d like to admit. I’ll hear two colleagues talking in the hallway, or a parent explaining something, and I’ll jump in because in my head I’m thinking, “Oh, I know how to help with this,” or “Let me clarify that.” But then I realize I’ve talked over them or kind of taken charge before they even finished their sentence.

It happens at home too—my spouse might be talking with a relative, and I’ll butt in like I’m solving the problem, when nobody asked me to. I don’t mean it as rude, but it comes out that way sometimes.
Do you often find yourself acting on impulse, like doing things without thinking them through?

Um… acting on impulse. I’m not totally sure how to answer that, honestly. I mean, I make quick decisions sometimes, but I don’t know if I’d call it “without thinking.” 

Like, in teaching you’re constantly reacting—one kid needs help, another situation pops up, the schedule changes—so you sort of have to move fast. And then I start thinking about how schools expect you to be flexible but also have everything planned, which is its own whole thing…

Sorry, I’m getting off track. I guess I’d need an example of what you mean by impulse. I’m not sure I’ve noticed that as a big thing.
Do you often act on impulse in your personal life, outside of work or teaching?

Outside of work… I’m not sure. I mean, probably everybody does that sometimes, right? Like buying something without really comparing prices, or saying yes to a dinner before checking the calendar—but I don’t know if that’s what you mean by impulsive.

At home I tend to… well, actually, my wife would probably have a better answer to this than I do. She notices things before I do. Like I’ll start a house project because something is bothering me, and then suddenly the garage is a mess, and I’m looking for a tool I know I had in 1998—sorry, that’s not really answering.

I guess I don’t clearly think of myself as “acting on impulse” in my personal life. I’d need you to define it a little more, because I’m not sure what counts.
Have you ever had problems in your personal relationships due to saying or doing something without thinking it through?

Yeah… I think so. Not like I’m trying to be hurtful, but I’ll jump into conversations—like my wife talking with a relative, or at work with colleagues or parents—and in my head I’m thinking, “Oh, I can help,” or “I know what they mean,” and then I’m already talking before they’re done.

And then it turns into me taking over the conversation, which… yeah, people don’t always appreciate that. My wife will give me that look, like, “Let them finish,” and I realize I kind of barged in. It causes tension because I think I’m helping, but it comes across like I’m not listening or I’m trying to run the whole thing.
Do you often have trouble completing tasks or projects you've started?

I’m not sure how to answer that one. I mean… tasks and projects, that could mean a lot of things. At work there are always things that are “started” but not really finished because somebody changes the plan, or the meeting gets moved, or a student needs something right then.

At home, I guess I have projects that sit around, but I don’t know if that’s unusual. Like, there’s always something half-done in a house, right? You fix one thing and then notice the drawer sticks, and then you’re in the garage looking for screws, and then—well, anyway.

I wouldn’t say I’ve clearly noticed it as a major problem, but I might need a more specific example of what you mean by “trouble completing.”
Do you often find yourself easily distracted by things around you?

Easily distracted by things around me… I’m not sure. I mean, it depends where I am, I guess. If there’s a lot going on, like noise in the hallway or someone moving around, I notice it, but I don’t know if that’s more than other people.

At school there’s always something happening—kids coming in and out, announcements, papers, somebody needing a pen—and so it’s hard to separate “I’m distracted” from “the room is just busy.” At home, too, my wife will say something while I’m looking for my glasses, and then I’ll notice the mail on the counter, and then—sorry, I’m wandering.

I guess I don’t have a clear answer. I notice things around me, but I don’t know if I’d call it a big problem unless you mean something specific.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting or feeling restless when you're sitting still?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, I don’t always notice it at first, which is the weird part. Like in IEP meetings, or those admin classes I have to sit through, I’ll realize my leg has been bouncing under the table the whole time, or I’m clicking a pen over and over.

Sometimes I’m shifting around in the chair so much that people glance over, and then I’m like, oh—okay, I’m doing it again. It’s not like I’m trying to be disruptive. Sitting still just feels… I don’t know, uncomfortable after a while. And those meetings can go on forever, with paperwork and goals and accommodations—sorry, I’m getting off track—but yes, the fidgeting happens a lot.
Do you often have trouble waiting for your turn in line or in conversations?

Waiting my turn… I don’t know. In a line, I mean, I don’t love lines, but who does? If I’m at the grocery store and someone’s using coupons or there’s a price check, I’ll notice myself getting kind of impatient, but I don’t know if that’s unusual or just being a person with frozen food in the cart.

In conversations… maybe sometimes I jump in if I think I know where someone’s going, but I’m not sure that’s the same as “trouble waiting.” With teachers we’re always sort of overlapping—somebody mentions a student, then somebody else remembers a meeting, then the bell rings, and it’s all a little chaotic anyway.

So… I guess I’m not really sure. I haven’t thought of it as a big issue, but maybe I’d need an example of what you mean.
Do you often have trouble organizing your tasks or activities?

Organizing tasks or activities… I’m not sure how to answer that. I mean, my work has a lot of moving parts—lesson plans, paperwork, meetings, emails, student schedules—and some of that is just the job, you know? Special ed is basically a stack of folders that somehow keeps growing.

I do use lists sometimes, but then I’ll have three different lists—one on a sticky note, one in my planner, one in my head—and then the sticky note ends up in a folder with something totally unrelated. Actually, yesterday I found a note from last month tucked into a packet about bus schedules, and I don’t even know why I put it there.

But I don’t know if that means I have “trouble organizing” in the way you mean. I usually get things done eventually. It can feel messy getting there, though.
Do you often dominate conversations with friends or family members outside of work?

Outside of work? Yeah… I mean, probably. My wife would say yes faster than I would.

I’ll start answering a simple question, like about dinner plans or something, and then I’m explaining the whole background of why I think the new grocery store layout is strange—actually they moved the bread aisle recently and it makes no sense—but, yeah, I can kind of take over without meaning to.

It happens at work too, maybe that’s where I notice it more. I’ll go into a parent conference or a staff meeting meaning to be brief, and then suddenly I hear myself giving three examples, a story from my classroom, and suggestions nobody asked for, and the other person is clearly trying to wrap it up. Then I’m like, okay, I should stop talking now. But I don’t always catch it in time.
Do you often blurt out answers before questions have been completed in conversations with friends or family?

Yeah… yes, I do that. I don’t always notice it until I’m already halfway into my answer.

Like with my wife, if she’s talking to one of our relatives and I think I know what she’s trying to explain, I’ll jump in and start “helping,” but really I’m talking over her. Or with parents at school, they’ll start asking something and before they even finish the question, I’m already answering or steering the conversation because I think I know where it’s going.

And then sometimes I realize, oh, they weren’t done. I kind of took charge there. I don’t mean it in a rude way, but it happens a lot.
Did you have any problems with impulsivity or behavior when you were a child?

Oh yeah, that goes way back. My mother used to joke that I “taught the class from my seat” in elementary school, because I was always popping out of my chair or talking when I wasn’t supposed to.

And I’d cut in before the teacher even finished giving directions—like I already knew what she was going to say, even when I probably didn’t. I think about that now with my own students sometimes, actually, how teachers must have handled kids like me back then… but yes, it wasn’t something that just showed up later in life. That was kind of me from early on.
Have you ever been in a situation where you felt like you couldn't control your impulses, even when you knew it might cause problems?

Yeah, definitely. The main thing that comes to mind is conversations. I’ll know I should wait—like I can literally be thinking, “Don’t jump in, let them finish”—and then I’m already talking.

It happens with colleagues, with parents at school, and at home too. My wife might be talking to a relative, and I think I’m helping by clarifying something or moving the conversation along, but really I’ve taken over before either of them has finished. Same with a parent meeting—I hear the first half of a question and I’m off answering what I think they’re asking.

And then afterward I feel bad, because I can see that I talked over them or kind of grabbed the steering wheel. I know it can cause problems, but in the moment it’s like my mouth gets there before the rest of me does.
Do you often have trouble sustaining focus during tasks or activities that you're not particularly interested in?

I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean… if I’m interested in something, I can stay with it pretty well, sometimes too long, honestly. But if it’s something I don’t care about, I don’t know—I'd have to think about examples.

Like paperwork at school can be rough, but everybody hates paperwork, right? Special ed paperwork is its own whole universe, and half the time the forms change or somebody wants it worded a certain way… sorry, I’m getting off track.

I guess I haven’t really paid attention to whether it’s a focus issue exactly, or just that some tasks are boring and I put them off. So I’m not sure.
Have you experienced these kinds of symptoms, like not being able to slow down or interrupting others, consistently throughout your adult life?

Well, not consistently throughout all of adulthood, no—not at this level. I mean, I’ve always been kind of a fast talker, and my wife would probably have opinions about that, but the real trouble with it feeling like I can’t slow myself down has been more recent.

I’d say it’s been about eight months now, since our older relative moved in with us. That kind of changed the whole rhythm of the house—mealtimes, conversations, who’s needing what—and I think that’s when it started feeling much harder to manage.
Have these symptoms, like interrupting others or not being able to slow down, caused any significant problems for you at work or in your relationships?

Yeah… unfortunately, yes. At work it’s gotten pretty serious. I mean, schools are stressful places anyway—there’s always some new form, some new meeting, someone needing something five minutes ago—but this has gone past just “he talks too much.”

I’ve had enough complaints that they put me on a corrective plan. That was… humiliating, honestly. Because in my head I’m trying to help, trying to keep things moving, but what people experience is me cutting them off or taking over.

And at home it’s affecting things too. My wife has said the caregiving routines are harder because everybody’s already managing a lot, and then they also have to manage my energy on top of it. That one hurt to hear.

So yes, it’s causing problems. I feel like I’m damaging trust with colleagues and with my family, even though that’s the opposite of what I’m trying to do.
Have you experienced significant symptoms of inattention, such as making careless mistakes or having difficulty sustaining focus, in addition to your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity?

I don’t know that I can say yes to that. I mean, I make mistakes like anybody does, especially when there are a hundred little pieces to track, but I haven’t really thought of that as the main problem.

Focus is tricky because with teaching, your attention is getting pulled all over the place anyway—one student needs something, someone’s calling from the office, there’s a behavior plan, then an email, then you’re supposed to document it all, and suddenly you’re eating lunch at 2:15. Sorry, that’s probably not what you asked.

I guess… no, I haven’t really noticed major inattention symptoms on top of the other stuff. Or at least I’m not sure how to separate that from just the normal chaos of the job.
Have you experienced symptoms like interrupting others, fidgeting, or blurting out answers consistently since you were a child?

Yeah, that part goes way back. My mother used to joke that in elementary school I was practically teaching the class from my seat, because I was always up, talking, or jumping in before the teacher even finished giving directions.

I remember her saying it like it was funny—kind of one of those family stories that gets repeated at holidays, you know, along with the burnt turkey story and my uncle’s terrible driving directions—but there was truth in it. I wasn’t suddenly like this as an adult. The current stress at home made it harder to contain, but the talking out of turn and not staying in my seat… that was part of me as a kid too.

doctor.question: Have you ever been in a situation where you felt like you couldn't control your impulses, even when you knew it might cause problems?

target_item.name: Interrupting_Intruding
target_item.manifestation: I keep jumping into conversations between colleagues, parents, or my spouse and our relative because I think I’m helping, but I end up talking over them or taking charge before they’ve even had a chance to finish.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about difficulty controlling impulses in situations where it may cause problems, which most directly matches interrupting or intruding on others despite knowing it can be disruptive.

patient.answer:
Yeah, definitely. The main thing that comes to mind is conversations. I’ll know I should wait—like I can literally be thinking, “Don’t jump in, let them finish”—and then I’m already talking.

It happens with colleagues, with parents at school, and at home too. My wife might be talking to a relative, and I think I’m helping by clarifying something or moving the conversation along, but really I’ve taken over before either of them has finished. Same with a parent meeting—I hear the first half of a question and I’m off answering what I think they’re asking.

And then afterward I feel bad, because I can see that I talked over them or kind of grabbed the steering wheel. I know it can cause problems, but in the moment it’s like my mouth gets there before the rest of me does.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of persistent patterns of inattention
doctor.question: Do you often have trouble sustaining focus during tasks or activities that you're not particularly interested in?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty sustaining attention during uninteresting tasks, which is an inattention symptom. The provided symptom profile only covers hyperactive/impulsive symptoms and related requirements, not sustained focus.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean… if I’m interested in something, I can stay with it pretty well, sometimes too long, honestly. But if it’s something I don’t care about, I don’t know—I'd have to think about examples.

Like paperwork at school can be rough, but everybody hates paperwork, right? Special ed paperwork is its own whole universe, and half the time the forms change or somebody wants it worded a certain way… sorry, I’m getting off track.

I guess I haven’t really paid attention to whether it’s a focus issue exactly, or just that some tasks are boring and I put them off. So I’m not sure.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms have been persistent across their lifetime
doctor.question: Have you experienced these kinds of symptoms, like not being able to slow down or interrupting others, consistently throughout your adult life?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This level of trouble has been going on for about 8 months, since our older relative moved in with us.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about how long and how consistently these symptoms have been present; this profile covers the current duration of the trouble.

patient.answer:
Well, not consistently throughout all of adulthood, no—not at this level. I mean, I’ve always been kind of a fast talker, and my wife would probably have opinions about that, but the real trouble with it feeling like I can’t slow myself down has been more recent.

I’d say it’s been about eight months now, since our older relative moved in with us. That kind of changed the whole rhythm of the house—mealtimes, conversations, who’s needing what—and I think that’s when it started feeling much harder to manage.

doctor.intent: Determine if symptoms have caused significant impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Have these symptoms, like interrupting others or not being able to slow down, caused any significant problems for you at work or in your relationships?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: At work, the complaints have gotten serious enough that I was put on a corrective plan, and at home my spouse says caregiving routines are harder because people have to manage my energy on top of everything else. I feel like I’m damaging trust with colleagues and family even though I’m trying to help.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the symptoms have caused significant problems at work or in relationships, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yeah… unfortunately, yes. At work it’s gotten pretty serious. I mean, schools are stressful places anyway—there’s always some new form, some new meeting, someone needing something five minutes ago—but this has gone past just “he talks too much.”

I’ve had enough complaints that they put me on a corrective plan. That was… humiliating, honestly. Because in my head I’m trying to help, trying to keep things moving, but what people experience is me cutting them off or taking over.

And at home it’s affecting things too. My wife has said the caregiving routines are harder because everybody’s already managing a lot, and then they also have to manage my energy on top of it. That one hurt to hear.

So yes, it’s causing problems. I feel like I’m damaging trust with colleagues and with my family, even though that’s the opposite of what I’m trying to do.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a specific attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) subtype
doctor.question: Have you experienced significant symptoms of inattention, such as making careless mistakes or having difficulty sustaining focus, in addition to your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about inattentive symptoms such as careless mistakes or difficulty sustaining focus. The provided symptom profile only covers hyperactive/impulsive symptoms, duration, impairment, and childhood onset, not inattention.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I can say yes to that. I mean, I make mistakes like anybody does, especially when there are a hundred little pieces to track, but I haven’t really thought of that as the main problem.

Focus is tricky because with teaching, your attention is getting pulled all over the place anyway—one student needs something, someone’s calling from the office, there’s a behavior plan, then an email, then you’re supposed to document it all, and suddenly you’re eating lunch at 2:15. Sorry, that’s probably not what you asked.

I guess… no, I haven’t really noticed major inattention symptoms on top of the other stuff. Or at least I’m not sure how to separate that from just the normal chaos of the job.

doctor.intent: Determine if symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity have been persistent since childhood
doctor.question: Have you experienced symptoms like interrupting others, fidgeting, or blurting out answers consistently since you were a child?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: My mother used to joke that even in elementary school I taught the class from my seat because I was always out of my chair, talking, or cutting in before the teacher finished directions. This was part of who I was long before adulthood, not something that just started with this family change.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether hyperactive/impulsive symptoms were present consistently since childhood, which directly maps to onset prior to age 12 years.

patient.answer:
Yeah, that part goes way back. My mother used to joke that in elementary school I was practically teaching the class from my seat, because I was always up, talking, or jumping in before the teacher even finished giving directions.

I remember her saying it like it was funny—kind of one of those family stories that gets repeated at holidays, you know, along with the burnt turkey story and my uncle’s terrible driving directions—but there was truth in it. I wasn’t suddenly like this as an adult. The current stress at home made it harder to contain, but the talking out of turn and not staying in my seat… that was part of me as a kid too.
